title: Brokers, Prop Firms & Accounts
hook: Know the difference before you fund an account.

launchpad.outcome: Explain what a broker account, a prop firm evaluation, and a simulated account each actually test.
launchpad.missionQuestion: If a trader wants to prove she's consistent before risking real money, which account type actually answers that?

markers.label: Broker vs. prop firm vs. simulated
Matching the account to the goal

slides.kicker: Every account is either your money, someone else's, or practice money
slides.title: Three kinds of accounts

items.label: Broker account
items.desc: Trades your own capital, you keep every dollar of profit and absorb every dollar of loss.

items.label: Prop firm evaluation
items.desc: Access to their capital if you prove you can trade within their rules, profits usually split once funded.

items.label: Simulated account
items.desc: No real money at all, pure practice, zero financial risk.

slides.kicker: Match the account to the goal
slides.body: A trader wants to test whether her execution is consistent before risking real money.

check.prompt: Which account type actually answers that question?

options.label: Jump straight to a funded account
options.feedback: Skipping straight to funded capital without proving consistency first is a real risk.

options.label: A simulated (demo) account
options.why: Right. Simulated accounts exist to prove consistency with zero financial risk.

slides.quote: I'm not telling you which account type to start with. I'm telling you to know exactly which one you're in, and what that account expects from you, before you place a single trade.

slides.body: A trader passes a prop firm's evaluation and gets funded.

check.prompt: Whose capital is she now trading, and what does that change about her risk?

options.label: Her own capital, the evaluation was just a formality
options.feedback: The whole point of an evaluation is that it isn't a formality, it decides whether she trades her own money or the firm's.

options.label: Nobody's capital, funded accounts are simulated
options.feedback: A funded account trades the firm's real capital, not a simulation.

options.label: The firm's capital, her personal money isn't directly at risk, but she now trades inside the firm's rules
options.why: Funded status shifts whose money is at risk but adds real rule constraints in exchange.

slides.prompt: Imagine another AGHF member asks: "Should I just go straight for a funded prop account?" How would you explain the trade-offs to them?
slides.modelAnswer: A funded prop account means trading someone else's capital under their rules, without having proven yet that your execution is consistent. Going straight there skips the step where a simulated account lets you prove consistency with zero financial risk first, and most people fail an evaluation not because they don't know the market, but because they haven't proven their own discipline yet.

takeaways: A broker account risks your own capital from trade one.
A prop evaluation tests rule-discipline before granting capital access.
A simulated account proves consistency with zero financial risk.
remember: Know exactly which account you're in, and what it expects from you.
